text:
How Two Strangers Agree on a Secret in Public

The problem

Alice and Bob want to share a secret number. They will use it as a key to scramble their messages. The only channel they have is a line that anyone can hear: a phone line that might be recorded, or a public network. Eve, the eavesdropper, hears everything they say.

If Alice simply tells Bob "my secret is 42", Eve now knows it too. So the secret cannot travel over the line. It has to end up in both Alice's and Bob's hands without ever being spoken. That sounds impossible, but mathematics offers a way, provided there is an operation that is easy to do and hard to undo. Public-key key exchange, in its best-known form called Diffie-Hellman after its 1976 inventors, is built on exactly that kind of operation.

Clock arithmetic

Start with a clock. If it is 10 o'clock and five hours pass, it is 3 o'clock, because the clock wraps around after 12. Mathematicians write this as 10 + 5 = 3 (mod 12), read "10 plus 5 is 3, modulo 12". Multiplication works the same way: you multiply as normal, then wrap the answer back into the range.

Now use a clock with 17 positions, numbered 0 to 16. Take 3 and keep multiplying by 3, wrapping each time you pass 16:

3, then 9, then 27 becomes 10, then 30 becomes 13, then 39 becomes 5, then 15, then 45 becomes 11.

So 3 multiplied by itself seven times, on this clock, gives 11. We write 3^7 mod 17 = 11.

Now try the reverse problem. Someone tells you that 3 raised to some unknown power gives 13 on the 17-clock, and asks what the power is. With 17 positions you can simply try every power from 1 to 16, which takes a few seconds by hand. But imagine the clock had 600 digits and the exponent was similarly huge. Going forward is still quick, because a computer can square numbers repeatedly. Raising 3 to the millionth power takes only about twenty squarings. Going backward, finding the exponent from the result, is called the discrete logarithm problem, and no known method solves it in any practical time at that size. This gap between easy forward steps and very hard reverse steps is the foundation of everything that follows.

Agreeing on public numbers

Alice and Bob first agree on two numbers in the open. One is a prime p, the size of the clock, here 17. The other is a base g, here 3. Eve is allowed to know both. Nothing secret has been said yet.

Each person now picks a private number and publishes a scrambled version of it.

Alice secretly picks a = 4. She computes A = 3^4 mod 17. Working through the powers, 3^4 is 81, and 81 wrapped onto the 17-clock is 13. She sends 13 to Bob.

Bob secretly picks b = 6. He computes B = 3^6 mod 17, which is 729 wrapped onto the clock, giving 15. He sends 15 to Alice.

Eve now has 17, 3, 13 and 15. Everything that was spoken is in her hands.

The shared secret appears

Alice receives Bob's number, 15. She raises it to her own secret power, 4: she computes 15^4 mod 17. Since 15 is the same as -2 on this clock, and (-2)^4 = 16, her result is 16.

Bob receives Alice's number, 13. He raises it to his own secret power, 6: he computes 13^6 mod 17. Since 13^2 = 169, which wraps to 16, we get 13^6 = 16^3, and 16 is the same as -1, so (-1)^3 = -1, which is 16 on this clock.

Both of them have 16. Neither sent it. It was never on the line.

Why this always works

Alice's calculation is really (3^6)^4, which is 3^24, because she raised Bob's public number to her private power. Bob's calculation is (3^4)^6, which is also 3^24, because he raised Alice's public number to his private power. Both expressions reduce to the same thing through the school rule that (x^m)^n = x^(mn), and that is the whole trick. Multiplying a by b gives the same result as multiplying b by a, so the two private numbers combine into one shared quantity that each side can compute, but neither could compute alone from the public information. Each person has one private half of the recipe and the other person's public half, and the two halves meet in the same answer.

Why Eve is stuck

Eve knows 3, 17, 13 and 15. The shared secret is 3^(4 x 6) mod 17. To get it directly from the public numbers, she would need to find Alice's secret power a from 13, or Bob's power b from 15. Those are discrete logarithm problems. On a 17-clock she could brute force them. On a real system she cannot. Nobody has proven that there is no faster way than brute force to get the shared secret from the public numbers, but decades of attempts have failed, and the security of the scheme rests on that belief.

Real systems use much bigger numbers. A common choice uses a prime of about 2048 bits, which is roughly 617 decimal digits. Another common choice, used in modern systems such as TLS 1.3 and the messaging app Signal, uses elliptic curves, where the numbers are 256 bits long and the arithmetic is more intricate but follows the same logic. The private numbers are chosen randomly, and the strength of the whole scheme depends on that randomness. After the shared value is computed, it is passed through a hash function to produce a key of the right length for encryption.

Limits and caveats

The basic exchange has a weakness. It proves nothing about who is on the other end. An attacker, sometimes called Mallory, can sit in the middle: she runs one exchange with Alice, pretending to be Bob, and another with Bob, pretending to be Alice. Each of them thinks they have a secret shared with the other, but each secret is actually shared with Mallory. The fix is authentication. In TLS, a certificate issued by a trusted authority vouches that the public numbers belong to the real server. In Signal, users can compare a short safety code in person, which confirms that no one has swapped their keys.

Another refinement is forward secrecy. If Alice and Bob generate new private numbers for every conversation and discard them afterwards, then even if someone records the traffic and later steals a long-term key, they still cannot decrypt past sessions.

Finally, there is a long-term caveat. The discrete logarithm problem is easy for a sufficiently large quantum computer, using an algorithm published by Peter Shor in 1994. Such machines do not yet exist at the needed scale, but the threat is serious enough that standards bodies have been designing and deploying post-quantum key exchange methods that rely on different hard problems.

Summary

Two people who have never met can agree on a secret over a public line because they do not send the secret. They send only scrambled versions of their private choices, computed with an operation that is easy in one direction and hard to reverse. Each combines their own private choice with the other's public value, and because the order of multiplication does not matter, both arrive at the same number. An eavesdropper who hears everything still faces the hard reverse problem. The scheme is simple in its core idea, and the real work lies in choosing huge numbers, random secrets and proper identity checks.
